claim: Drosophila larvae have a small number of gustatory sense neurons.
source: Despite the small number of gustatory sense neurons, Drosophila larvae are able to sense a wide range of chemicals.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a premise for the study.

claim: Drosophila larvae are able to sense a wide range of chemicals.
source: Despite the small number of gustatory sense neurons, Drosophila larvae are able to sense a wide range of chemicals.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Evidence for taste multimodality has been provided in single neurons.
source: Although evidence for taste multimodality has been provided in single neurons, an overview of gustatory responses at the periphery is missing and hereby we explore whole-organ calcium imaging of the external taste center.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and references prior work, though specific citations are not provided in this sentence.

claim: Neurons can be activated by different combinations of taste modalities, including opposite hedonic valence.
source: We find that neurons can be activated by different combinations of taste modalities, including opposite hedonic valence and identify distinct temporal dynamics of response.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Distinct temporal dynamics of response exist in larval taste neurons.
source: We find that neurons can be activated by different combinations of taste modalities, including opposite hedonic valence and identify distinct temporal dynamics of response.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by calcium imaging data.

claim: Sweet sensing has not been fully characterized in the external larval gustatory organ.
source: Although sweet sensing has not been fully characterized so far in the external larval gustatory organ, we recorded responses elicited by sugar.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Responses elicited by sugar were recorded in the external larval gustatory organ.
source: Although sweet sensing has not been fully characterized so far in the external larval gustatory organ, we recorded responses elicited by sugar.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by calcium imaging data.

claim: Larval sugar sensing relies on the Gr43a pharyngeal receptor.
source: Previous findings established that larval sugar sensing relies on the Gr43a pharyngeal receptor, but the question remains if external neurons contribute to this taste.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and references previous findings from the literature.

claim: External and internal gustation use distinct and complementary mechanisms in sugar sensing.
source: Here, we postulate that external and internal gustation use distinct and complementary mechanisms in sugar sensing and we identify external sucrose sensing neurons.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by behavioral and imaging data.

claim: External sucrose sensing neurons have been identified.
source: Here, we postulate that external and internal gustation use distinct and complementary mechanisms in sugar sensing and we identify external sucrose sensing neurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in the manuscript.

claim: Drosophila larvae comprise only few chemosensory neurons at the periphery.
source: Despite comprising only few chemosensory neurons at the periphery (Stocker, 1994; Stocker, 2008), Drosophila larvae are able to sense a wide range of chemicals but the principles of how a small neuronal population encodes a large sensory space entail unresolved questions (Komarov and Sprecher, 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Drosophila larvae display behaviors to different gustatory cues.
source: They display behaviors to different gustatory cues (Gerber and Stocker, 2007), being repelled by bitter tastants (El-Keredy et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2016) as possible signals of toxic food, and attracted by sweet, certain amino acids (Schipanski et al., 2008; Croset et al., 2016; Kudow et al., 2017), or ribonucleosides (Mishra et al., 2018), indicators of a nutritious diet.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple supporting citations.

claim: Drosophila larvae are repelled by bitter tastants.
source: They display behaviors to different gustatory cues (Gerber and Stocker, 2007), being repelled by bitter tastants (El-Keredy et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2016) as possible signals of toxic food, and attracted by sweet, certain amino acids (Schipanski et al., 2008; Croset et al., 2016; Kudow et al., 2017), or ribonucleosides (Mishra et al., 2018), indicators of a nutritious diet.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Drosophila larvae are attracted by sweet tastants.
source: They display behaviors to different gustatory cues (Gerber and Stocker, 2007), being repelled by bitter tastants (El-Keredy et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2016) as possible signals of toxic food, and attracted by sweet, certain amino acids (Schipanski et al., 2008; Croset et al., 2016; Kudow et al., 2017), or ribonucleosides (Mishra et al., 2018), indicators of a nutritious diet.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Drosophila larvae are attracted by certain amino acids.
source: They display behaviors to different gustatory cues (Gerber and Stocker, 2007), being repelled by bitter tastants (El-Keredy et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2016) as possible signals of toxic food, and attracted by sweet, certain amino acids (Schipanski et al., 2008; Croset et al., 2016; Kudow et al., 2017), or ribonucleosides (Mishra et al., 2018), indicators of a nutritious diet.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Drosophila larvae are attracted by ribonucleosides.
source: They display behaviors to different gustatory cues (Gerber and Stocker, 2007), being repelled by bitter tastants (El-Keredy et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2016) as possible signals of toxic food, and attracted by sweet, certain amino acids (Schipanski et al., 2008; Croset et al., 2016; Kudow et al., 2017), or ribonucleosides (Mishra et al., 2018), indicators of a nutritious diet.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Drosophila larvae increase body size up to 200–250-fold in 5 days.
source: For Drosophila larvae, an animal that increases body size up to 200–250-fold in 5 days (Robertson, 2009) and spends the bulk of its time searching for food (Green et al., 1983), the most important nutritional sources are sugar, such as sucrose and fructose found in fermenting fruits – their natural diet, as well as proteins and fatty acids, taken up from yeast growing on this substrate.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Drosophila larvae spend the bulk of their time searching for food.
source: For Drosophila larvae, an animal that increases body size up to 200–250-fold in 5 days (Robertson, 2009) and spends the bulk of its time searching for food (Green et al., 1983), the most important nutritional sources are sugar, such as sucrose and fructose found in fermenting fruits – their natural diet, as well as proteins and fatty acids, taken up from yeast growing on this substrate.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The most important nutritional sources for Drosophila larvae are sugar, proteins, and fatty acids.
source: For Drosophila larvae, an animal that increases body size up to 200–250-fold in 5 days (Robertson, 2009) and spends the bulk of its time searching for food (Green et al., 1983), the most important nutritional sources are sugar, such as sucrose and fructose found in fermenting fruits – their natural diet, as well as proteins and fatty acids, taken up from yeast growing on this substrate.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction based on established knowledge.

claim: Larval external taste neurons have not been associated with a role in sugar taste preference.
source: Nevertheless, larval external taste neurons have not been associated thus far to a role in sugar taste preference.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a gap in knowledge.

claim: Taste encoding at the periphery in the fruit fly has been described in line with segregated hedonic valence logic.
source: In the fruit fly, taste encoding at the periphery has been described in line with segregated hedonic valence logic, attractive and aversive taste being detected through separate cell populations.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and references established knowledge in the field.

claim: Attractive and aversive taste are detected through separate cell populations in the fruit fly.
source: In the fruit fly, taste encoding at the periphery has been described in line with segregated hedonic valence logic, attractive and aversive taste being detected through separate cell populations.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and references established knowledge.

claim: Specific members of the Gustatory receptors (GRs) family mediate sweet or bitter taste.
source: Accordingly, specific members of the Gustatory receptors (GRs) family mediate sweet or bitter taste, namely cells expressing Gr5a, Gr61a, or Gr64a-f detect sugars and do not overlap with bitter-taste cells expressing Gr66a or Gr33a (Dahanukar et al., 2007; Fujii et al., 2015; Thorne et al., 2004; Liman et al., 2014; French et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Cells expressing Gr5a, Gr61a, or Gr64a-f detect sugars.
source: Accordingly, specific members of the Gustatory receptors (GRs) family mediate sweet or bitter taste, namely cells expressing Gr5a, Gr61a, or Gr64a-f detect sugars and do not overlap with bitter-taste cells expressing Gr66a or Gr33a (Dahanukar et al., 2007; Fujii et al., 2015; Thorne et al., 2004; Liman et al., 2014; French et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Sugar-detecting cells do not overlap with bitter-taste cells expressing Gr66a or Gr33a.
source: Accordingly, specific members of the Gustatory receptors (GRs) family mediate sweet or bitter taste, namely cells expressing Gr5a, Gr61a, or Gr64a-f detect sugars and do not overlap with bitter-taste cells expressing Gr66a or Gr33a (Dahanukar et al., 2007; Fujii et al., 2015; Thorne et al., 2004; Liman et al., 2014; French et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Additional taste modalities partially overlap onto sweet and bitter cells by means of added-on expression of Ionotropic receptors (IRs) or pickpocket receptors (Ppk).
source: Additional taste modalities such as salt, fatty acid, carbonation, polyamines, or amino acids partially overlap onto these by means of added-on expression of Ionotropic receptors (IRs) or pickpocket receptors (Ppk) (Zhang et al., 2013; Hussain et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2017; Tauber et al., 2017; Ahn et al., 2017; Ganguly et al., 2017; Sánchez-Alcañiz et al., 2018; Jaeger et al., 2018), but maintaining a segregated attraction/aversion quality of taste in the separate cell populations.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: In Drosophila larva, taste of opposed valence can overlap in a single gustatory receptor neuron (GRN).
source: Contrary to described adult fly taste sensing logic, in Drosophila larva taste of opposed valence can overlap, shown by a single gustatory receptor neuron (GRN) activated by both sugar and bitter tastants (van Giesen et al., 2016a) and thereby indicating a higher level of taste integration than in the adult fly.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: A single gustatory receptor neuron (GRN) can be activated by both sugar and bitter tastants in Drosophila larva.
source: Contrary to described adult fly taste sensing logic, in Drosophila larva taste of opposed valence can overlap, shown by a single gustatory receptor neuron (GRN) activated by both sugar and bitter tastants (van Giesen et al., 2016a) and thereby indicating a higher level of taste integration than in the adult fly.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Drosophila larva shows a higher level of taste integration than the adult fly.
source: Contrary to described adult fly taste sensing logic, in Drosophila larva taste of opposed valence can overlap, shown by a single gustatory receptor neuron (GRN) activated by both sugar and bitter tastants (van Giesen et al., 2016a) and thereby indicating a higher level of taste integration than in the adult fly.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an inference from the cited data.

claim: Chemosensory organs are located at the tip of larval head.
source: Chemosensory organs are located at the tip of larval head, and comprise bipolar sensory neurons that extend axonal projections into defined regions of the brain (Figure 1A; Python and Stocker, 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Chemosensory organs comprise bipolar sensory neurons that extend axonal projections into defined regions of the brain.
source: Chemosensory organs are located at the tip of larval head, and comprise bipolar sensory neurons that extend axonal projections into defined regions of the brain (Figure 1A; Python and Stocker, 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: The terminal organ ganglion (TOG) has taste primary function.
source: The main external sense organs are the terminal organ ganglion (TOG) with taste primary function and the dorsal organ ganglion (DOG) as olfactory organ (Stocker, 1994; Klein et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The dorsal organ ganglion (DOG) is an olfactory organ.
source: The main external sense organs are the terminal organ ganglion (TOG) with taste primary function and the dorsal organ ganglion (DOG) as olfactory organ (Stocker, 1994; Klein et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Out of more than 30 GRNs in the TOG, only seven neuronal identities (C1–C7) have been mapped.
source: Out of more than 30 GRNs in the TOG only seven neuronal identities (C1–C7) have been mapped and are traceable by means of individual GR-Gal4 lines (Figure 1B; van Giesen et al., 2016a; Kwon et al., 2011; Rist and Thum, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Seven neuronal identities (C1–C7) are traceable by means of individual GR-Gal4 lines.
source: Out of more than 30 GRNs in the TOG only seven neuronal identities (C1–C7) have been mapped and are traceable by means of individual GR-Gal4 lines (Figure 1B; van Giesen et al., 2016a; Kwon et al., 2011; Rist and Thum, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Physiological characterization has been tackled in few single GRNs due to experimental restrictions.
source: Because of experimental restrictions in probing the system due to the limited availability of individually mapped TOG Gal4 lines, physiological characterization has been thus far tackled in few single GRNs, but a global approach for measuring responses in larval taste sense neurons could prove useful to an overview of peripheral gustatory responses.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as context for the study.

claim: Larval repertoire of taste receptors differs from expression described in adult flies.
source: Therewithal, larval repertoire of taste receptors differs from expression described in adult flies, with many GRs showing developmental stage-specificity.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction based on established knowledge.

claim: Many GRs show developmental stage-specificity.
source: Therewithal, larval repertoire of taste receptors differs from expression described in adult flies, with many GRs showing developmental stage-specificity.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction based on established knowledge.

claim: Gr66a/Gr33a-expressing neurons are present in the larva and have been associated with roles in bitter taste avoidance.
source: Gr66a/Gr33a-expressing neurons, mediators of bitter perception in the adult fly, are also present in the larva and have been associated with roles in bitter taste avoidance (Kim et al., 2016; Apostolopoulou et al., 2014; Choi et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Sweet sensing neurons or receptors have not been identified in the larval peripheral taste system.
source: However, sweet sensing neurons or receptors have not been identified in the larval peripheral taste system (Kwon et al., 2011), although larvae can detect and elicit behaviors towards most sugars (Rohwedder et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Larvae can detect and elicit behaviors towards most sugars.
source: However, sweet sensing neurons or receptors have not been identified in the larval peripheral taste system (Kwon et al., 2011), although larvae can detect and elicit behaviors towards most sugars (Rohwedder et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Larval sugar perception has been allotted to Gr43a fructose receptor.
source: Larval sugar perception has been allotted to Gr43a fructose receptor (Mishra et al., 2013), which, however, is expressed in pharyngeal sensory organs, foregut and in the brain, but absent from external taste neurons, similar to its expression in the adult fly where it acts as main hemolymph fructose sensor (Miyamoto et al., 2012; Miyamoto and Amrein, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Gr43a is expressed in pharyngeal sensory organs, foregut and in the brain, but absent from external taste neurons.
source: Larval sugar perception has been allotted to Gr43a fructose receptor (Mishra et al., 2013), which, however, is expressed in pharyngeal sensory organs, foregut and in the brain, but absent from external taste neurons, similar to its expression in the adult fly where it acts as main hemolymph fructose sensor (Miyamoto et al., 2012; Miyamoto and Amrein, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Gr43a acts as main hemolymph fructose sensor in the adult fly.
source: Larval sugar perception has been allotted to Gr43a fructose receptor (Mishra et al., 2013), which, however, is expressed in pharyngeal sensory organs, foregut and in the brain, but absent from external taste neurons, similar to its expression in the adult fly where it acts as main hemolymph fructose sensor (Miyamoto et al., 2012; Miyamoto and Amrein, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Sucrose can elicit physiological response in TOG neurons.
source: As one of the most important macronutrients in larval diet, and therefore it seems surprising that external taste organs at direct contact with animal's environment would not be involved in sugar detection and output behavior, all the more so as sucrose can elicit physiological response in TOG neurons (van Giesen et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Among all neurons responding to sugar group stimulation, 25.4% responded to both groups of mono and disaccharides.
source: Among all neurons responding to sugar group stimulation, a comparable ratio of cells showed activation to either one or the other category and 25.4% to both groups of mono and disaccharides.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 20% of salt-responding neurons responded to both low and high salt concentrations.
source: For salt-responding neurons, a higher proportion of neurons showed activation to high salt than to low salt concentration, and 20% neurons responded to both categories.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 38% of amino acid-responding neurons showed activation to two or more amino acid groups.
source: Amino acids split into four groups gave a rounded 62% of uni-group responses and the rest of 38% neurons responded to two or more amino acid groups per animal.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Within the total number of bitter-responsive neurons, 55% were uniquely activated by the DSoTC group.
source: Within the total number of bitter-responsive neurons, 55% were uniquely activated by the DSoTC group and respectively 30% by QLSC group.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: 30% of bitter-responsive neurons were uniquely activated by the QLSC group.
source: Within the total number of bitter-responsive neurons, 55% were uniquely activated by the DSoTC group and respectively 30% by QLSC group.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: 30.3% of taste cells responded to groups of both sweet and bitter modalities.
source: In animals stimulated with both modality groups, integration between sweet and bitter taste has been calculated and we observed similar proportions of taste cells responding only to bitter groups (30.3%), cells responding only to sugar (39.4%) and cells responding to groups of both modalities (30.3%).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: 68% of total responding neurons were activated by only one tastant per organ.
source: Total percentages of taste integration in pooled data are represented on the pie chart: 68% of total responding neurons were activated by only one tastant per organ and up to 32% of neurons responded to more than one tastant.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2D'.

claim: 32% of neurons responded to more than one tastant.
source: Total percentages of taste integration in pooled data are represented on the pie chart: 68% of total responding neurons were activated by only one tastant per organ and up to 32% of neurons responded to more than one tastant.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2D'.

claim: Most unimodal responses were recorded to sucrose and to high salt.
source: Most unimodal responses (uni-taste/cell, left extended pie) were recorded to sucrose and to high salt.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2D'.

claim: Response intensity of the C7 neuron to sucrose before denatonium presentation was not significantly different from responses after denatonium presentation.
source: Response intensity of the C7 neuron to sucrose before denatonium presentation was not significantly different from responses after denatonium presentation.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and supported by data shown in the figure.

claim: Tastants elicit different types of signals within the TOG organ, including ON responses, OFF responses, late activation, and fluorescence intensity drop.
source: However, at a closer look, tastants elicit different types of signals within the TOG organ, besides canonical ON response, neurons also showing OFF responses and late activation or even fluorescence intensity drop upon stimulation, as exemplified in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A for sucrose 500 mM, citric acid 100 mM, or NaCl 100 mM.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: CDL2 neuron was often recorded to respond with a decrease of fluorescence to citric acid.
source: In particular for citric acid, this neuron was often recorded to respond with a decrease of fluorescence while its neighbor, CDL1, typically showed canonical calcium activation to citric acid (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: CDL1 typically showed canonical calcium activation to citric acid.
source: In particular for citric acid, this neuron was often recorded to respond with a decrease of fluorescence while its neighbor, CDL1, typically showed canonical calcium activation to citric acid (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: C2-silencing showed a preference index different from controls for sucrose 500 mM.
source: Among the three probed neurons, only C2-silencing showed a preference index different from controls (Figure 4A, one-way ANOVA p<0.05), while C6 or C7 silencing did not show a notable behavioral defect.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: C6 or C7 silencing did not show a notable behavioral defect for sucrose preference.
source: Among the three probed neurons, only C2-silencing showed a preference index different from controls (Figure 4A, one-way ANOVA p<0.05), while C6 or C7 silencing did not show a notable behavioral defect.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: C2 neuron contributes to sucrose sensing.
source: Although all three neurons have previously been associated with physiological responses to sucrose 500 mM (van Giesen et al., 2016a), a defect in preference index to Sucrose 500 mM compared to control larvae is found only for C2 (p-value=0.038), indicating a direct contribution of this neuron in sucrose sensing.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 4A and supported by behavioral data.

claim: Larvae with C2 silenced show a greater defect for sugar preference on 2.5% agarose compared to 1% for all concentrations.
source: Larvae with C2 silenced show a greater defect for sugar preference on 2.5% agarose compared to 1% for all concentrations.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 4B and supported by behavioral data.

claim: Larvae rely at least partly on C2 in sucrose sensing on a denser substrate.
source: This suggests larvae rely at least partly on C2 in sucrose sensing on a denser substrate.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 4B as an inference from the behavioral data.

claim: At 1% agarose, C2 silencing has a lesser effect on sugar preference, suggesting that other mechanisms come into play for behavior on a softer substrate.
source: At 1%, C2 silencing has a lesser effect on sugar preference, suggesting that other mechanisms come into play for behavior on a softer substrate.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 4B as an inference from the behavioral data.

claim: Blue coloring of the intestine was observed as early as 2 min on 1% agarose.
source: Blue coloring of the intestine was observed as early as 2 min on 1% concentration, while on 2.5% animals didn't seem to be able to eat as easily as indicated by the lack of tint of their abdomen at 2 min and 5 min testing.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 4C and supported by the food ingestion test data.

claim: On 2.5% agarose, animals didn't seem to be able to eat as easily as indicated by the lack of tint of their abdomen at 2 min and 5 min testing.
source: Blue coloring of the intestine was observed as early as 2 min on 1% concentration, while on 2.5% animals didn't seem to be able to eat as easily as indicated by the lack of tint of their abdomen at 2 min and 5 min testing.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 4C and supported by the food ingestion test data.

claim: Animals easily eat the softer 1% food substrate but on denser 2.5% concentration ingestion is slower and evidently impaired especially for early test time points.
source: This suggests that animals easily eat the softer 1% food substrate but that on denser 2.5% concentration ingestion is slower and evidently impaired especially for early test time points.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 4C as an inference from the food ingestion test data.

claim: Optogenetic neuronal silencing of C2 using anion channelrhodopsin (GtACR1) expression led to an altered preference to sucrose 500 mM in larvae tested on 2.5%.
source: Optogenetic neuronal silencing of C2 using anion channelrhodopsin (GtACR1) expression (Mauss et al., 2017) (see Materials and methods) led to an altered preference to sucrose 500 mM in larvae tested on 2.5% (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: C2 and possibly other TOG neurons complement internal taste in sugar detection.
source: All in all, our observations subscribe to the hypothesis that C2 and possibly other TOG neurons complement internal taste in sugar detection and that larvae can use distinct sensing paths—pharyngeal neurons being employed for sugar taste during food ingestion, whereas external taste neurons are participating in sugar detection especially when eating is not accessible (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the behavioral and imaging data.

claim: Larvae can use distinct sensing paths—pharyngeal neurons being employed for sugar taste during food ingestion, whereas external taste neurons are participating in sugar detection especially when eating is not accessible.
source: All in all, our observations subscribe to the hypothesis that C2 and possibly other TOG neurons complement internal taste in sugar detection and that larvae can use distinct sensing paths—pharyngeal neurons being employed for sugar taste during food ingestion, whereas external taste neurons are participating in sugar detection especially when eating is not accessible (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the behavioral and imaging data.

claim: Roughly 60–70% versus 30–40% division of unimodal versus multimodal responding GRNs was observed.
source: For the tested substances at the concentrations chosen within this study, we observed roughly a 60–70% versus 30–40% division of unimodal versus multimodal responding GRNs (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1), comparable with tuning proportions reported for mouse fungiform taste sensing cells (Jisoo Han, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The tuning proportions observed are comparable with tuning proportions reported for mouse fungiform taste sensing cells.
source: For the tested substances at the concentrations chosen within this study, we observed roughly a 60–70% versus 30–40% division of unimodal versus multimodal responding GRNs (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1), comparable with tuning proportions reported for mouse fungiform taste sensing cells (Jisoo Han, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: 30% of neurons stimulated with bitters and sugars were activated by both taste groups.
source: Taste stimulation with substance-modality groups showed a mixed tuning of responding neurons and, in particular, 30% of neurons stimulated with bitters and sugars were activated by both taste groups, in accord with the integration of opposed valence cues in single larval neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by data presented earlier.

claim: Up to 68% of responsive neurons were activated by only one tastant per animal in animals stimulated with individual substances representative of different taste modalities.
source: Interestingly, in animals stimulated with individual substances representative of different taste modalities (Figure 2D), up to 68% of responsive neurons were activated by only one tastant per animal.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Distinct response dynamics elicited by tastants in larval GRNs include late neuronal activation characterized as OFF-response with onset after stimulus application.
source: An interesting feature in larval taste physiology revealed by our observations was related to distinct response dynamics elicited by tastants in larval GRNs. Apart from canonical GCaMP fluorescence increase during stimulus, we also identified late neuronal activation that could be characterized as OFF-response with onset after stimulus application, but also GCaMP fluorescence drop during taste stimulus as perhaps deactivation response.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by data presented earlier.

claim: GCaMP fluorescence drop during taste stimulus may represent deactivation response.
source: An interesting feature in larval taste physiology revealed by our observations was related to distinct response dynamics elicited by tastants in larval GRNs. Apart from canonical GCaMP fluorescence increase during stimulus, we also identified late neuronal activation that could be characterized as OFF-response with onset after stimulus application, but also GCaMP fluorescence drop during taste stimulus as perhaps deactivation response.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: Most notable deactivation signals were recorded in CDL2 neuron and most stereotypically to citric acid.
source: Most notable deactivation signals were recorded in CDL2 neuron and most stereotypically to citric acid (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Citric acid elicited concomitant activation in a neighboring cell named CDL1.
source: Interestingly, citric acid elicited concomitant activation in a neighboring cell named CDL1, indicating response patterns of activation-deactivation.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by data presented earlier.

claim: The synchronous activation coupled with deactivation responses in adjacent neurons resemble the description of ephaptic signaling.
source: The synchronous activation coupled with deactivation responses in adjacent neurons resemble the description of ephaptic signaling which implies that the electrical field of a responding cell generates hyperpolarization in the partner cell (Jefferys, 1995; Faber and Pereda, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as a speculative interpretation with supporting citations.

claim: Ephaptic transmission has been described in the olfactory system of the adult fly.
source: While ephaptic transmission has been described in the olfactory system of the adult fly (Su et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2019), it remains to be determined whether such lateral inhibition mechanism also occurs in Drosophila taste.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: A large proportion of neurons responsive to one taste substance per animal were activated by sucrose.
source: A large proportion of neurons responsive to one taste substance per animal were activated by sucrose and, interestingly, sucrose also elicited numerous responses in neurons activated by two or more tastants, in combinations such as sucrose+ citric acid, sucrose+ amino acid, sucrose+ high salt, and sucrose+ bitter (denatonium/quinine).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by data presented earlier.

claim: Sucrose elicited numerous responses in neurons activated by two or more tastants.
source: A large proportion of neurons responsive to one taste substance per animal were activated by sucrose and, interestingly, sucrose also elicited numerous responses in neurons activated by two or more tastants, in combinations such as sucrose+ citric acid, sucrose+ amino acid, sucrose+ high salt, and sucrose+ bitter (denatonium/quinine).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by data presented earlier.

claim: C7 has been linked to taste integration of opposed valence of sucrose and denatonium or quinine.
source: As expected, C7 has been linked to taste integration of opposed valence of sucrose and denatonium or quinine and we have not observed a defect in direct sucrose behavior in C7-silenced larvae (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: No defect in direct sucrose behavior was observed in C7-silenced larvae.
source: As expected, C7 has been linked to taste integration of opposed valence of sucrose and denatonium or quinine and we have not observed a defect in direct sucrose behavior in C7-silenced larvae (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Silencing C6 did not result in behavioral defects for sucrose preference.
source: Similarly, silencing C6 also did not result in behavioral defects.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by data presented earlier.

claim: C6 is known to have a role in CO2 sensing.
source: Known to have a role in CO2 sensing (Kwon et al., 2007; Jones et al., 2007; Faucher et al., 2006), C6 is likely not involved in sucrose behavioral response per se, but prospectively important for integration of this taste in detecting fermenting substrates, and therefore would also have a role in computing mixed tastes, a hypothesis to be confirmed by future work.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: C6 is likely not involved in sucrose behavioral response per se.
source: Known to have a role in CO2 sensing (Kwon et al., 2007; Jones et al., 2007; Faucher et al., 2006), C6 is likely not involved in sucrose behavioral response per se, but prospectively important for integration of this taste in detecting fermenting substrates, and therefore would also have a role in computing mixed tastes, a hypothesis to be confirmed by future work.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as an inference from the data.

claim: C2 contributes in the attraction to sucrose.
source: We identified C2 to contribute in the attraction to sucrose.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by behavioral data.

claim: Hernandez-Nunez et al., 2015 described a 'weak attractive response' in larvae when C2 was optogenetically activated alone.
source: Interestingly, Hernandez-Nunez et al., 2015 described a 'weak attractive response' in larvae when C2 was optogenetically activated alone but when co-activated together with C1 neuron, the C1-dependent repellent behavior was potentiated.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: When C2 was co-activated together with C1 neuron, the C1-dependent repellent behavior was potentiated.

claim: C2 neuron might be involved in sensing of an attractive cue while also enhancing the aversive behavior in association with a bitter neuron.

evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as an inference from cited data.

claim: Silencing C2 does not result in a complete abolishment of sucrose attraction.

evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as an inference from the behavioral data.

evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as a speculation based on the data.

claim: Silencing C5 neuron resulted in a trend for preference decrease compared to control larvae.
source: In support of this idea, we tested C5 neuron as a likely sugar-sensing candidate not expressing bitter-implicated receptors Gr66a/Gr33a, whose silencing also resulted in a trend for preference decrease compared to control larvae (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The Gr43a receptor expressed in pharyngeal sense neurons and in the brain has a central role in sugar sensing in larval taste.

evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: C2 neuron in the TOG senses sucrose and contributes to behavior prior to and in absence of eating.
source: Our results support the hypothesis that C2 neuron in the TOG senses sucrose and contributes to behavior prior to and in absence of eating, whereas Gr43a is the main sugar receptor but requires food ingestion.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as a conclusion from the data.

claim: Gr43a is the main sugar receptor but requires food ingestion.
source: Our results support the hypothesis that C2 neuron in the TOG senses sucrose and contributes to behavior prior to and in absence of eating, whereas Gr43a is the main sugar receptor but requires food ingestion.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as a conclusion from the data.

claim: The overrun of Gr43a guided behavior during food ingestion may be due to the lesser need for external sugar sensing when it has already been located and ingested.
source: The overrun of Gr43a guided behavior during food ingestion may be due to the lesser need for external sugar sensing when it has already been located and ingested, thus switching to an alternative internally guided pathway for sugar preference behavior (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: Gr43a expression in several internal tissues (pharynx, proventriculus, and brain) and its role as hemolymph fructose sensor may contribute to behavioral defects of Gr43a mutant to fructose sensing on 2.5% substrate.
source: Also, the reminiscent behavioral defects of Gr43a mutant to fructose sensing on 2.5% substrate (impaired ingestion) could be due to Gr43a expression in several internal tissues (pharynx, proventriculus, and brain) and to its role as hemolymph fructose sensor.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: Hemolymph carbohydrates influence larval feeding behavior through insulin signaling and SLC5A11.
source: It has been shown that hemolymph carbohydrates influence larval feeding behavior through insulin signaling and SLC5A11 (Ugrankar et al., 2018), but it remains to be determined if and how does a Gr43a mutant correlate with metabolic pathways and possibly interfere with sugar preference output behavior.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: In the adult, Gr43a acts as the main fructose hemolymph sensor but also associates a role in feeding suppression in satiated animals.

claim: Ir60b neurons carry a role in limiting sugar consumption.

claim: In the TOG, larvae detect quinine in C3 neuron.
source: The observations reported here in relation to taste sensing and cellular segregation of behavior can be paired with previous data for a depiction of sugar/bitter taste detection at the periphery (Mishra et al., 2013; Apostolopoulou et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2016; van Giesen et al., 2016a; Choi et al., 2016; Choi et al., 2020; Figure 5): in the TOG larvae detect quinine in C3 neuron, denatonium in C1, sucrose in C2 and C5, but also mix of sucrose and denatonium/quinine in C7 and also possibly a mix with sucrose in CO2-detector C6; at the level of pharyngeal neurons dietary sugar is sensed in DP4 (expressing Gr43a) and caffeine in DP1; in the brain, hemolymph sugar is detected by Gr43a receptor neurons.
